Debate coach's note, Friday. Written by Kishore Sir.

Ujjwal and Hemlata, both Class 12, were partners in today's inter-house debate. Last week they agreed Ujjwal would prepare rebuttals and Hemlata the opening. Today the opening was thin and there were no rebuttals at all. They lost to the house that came fourth last year.

Afterwards I spoke to each alone. Ujjwal said, "She always over-prepares, Sir. I thought she'd cover the rebuttals too." Hemlata said, "He's good at thinking on his feet. I thought he'd carry it if I did less." Both looked miserable, and a little angry with each other.

My next step: on Monday I'll sit them down together, show them both answers side by side, and have them write their parts on one sheet with dates.

qa.q: Which parts had Ujjwal and Hemlata agreed to prepare?
qa.a: Ujjwal would prepare the rebuttals and Hemlata the opening.

qa.q: What did each partner think about the other before the debate?
qa.a: Each felt relaxed about doing less, trusting the other to cover: Ujjwal assumed Hemlata would over-prepare, and Hemlata assumed Ujjwal would carry it on his feet.

qa.q: Why is showing them both answers side by side a useful next step?
qa.a: Seeing that each made the same bet would help them understand that both shirking made both lose, and writing parts with dates makes each accountable.

qa.q: How does the loss look to the rival house that won?
qa.a: They may be pleasantly surprised to beat a strong pair, not knowing the pair lost because each left the work to the other.

grounding: Two teenage debate partners each do less expecting the other to cover, so both lose, as recorded by their coach.

Trisha and Chandrika were paired for the presentation on water purification. They were given two weeks. When I checked in on Day 6, each told me separately that the other was "handling the slides."
